entries.clue: Posh boy and girl (2-2-2)

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
Ida is a girl's name, one of the short ones a grid keeps to hand

annotation.surface: An upper-class pair, a boy and a girl.
annotation.walkthrough: The join does not fall between the two people: the boy runs out after three letters and the girl begins there. La-di-da is mocking rather than admiring, said of someone putting on airs.
annotation.definitionFit: La-di-da describes affected upper-class speech and manners, which is the sneering sense of posh.

entries.clue: French king got attached to a woman (6)

blocks.note: France had eighteen kings called Louis, which is why the name is the one a grid reaches for
the clue's own article, written down as the single letter it is

annotation.surface: A French monarch who became fond of a lady.
annotation.walkthrough: The bare article taken as a letter is one of the quietest moves in the box, and it is easy to read straight past. Louisa is the English form of the name those kings handed on.
annotation.definitionFit: Louisa is a woman's given name, so the definition is the plain category the name belongs to.

entries.clue: Hamlet lacks silver when following noisy deer to Normandy resort (9)

indicatorNotes.noisy: Noisy points at the sound a word makes rather than the way it is spelt, so the next word is wanted for its noise.
indicatorNotes.lacks: To lack something is to be without it, so the letters named next are simply not there.
indicatorNotes.following: Following places the piece it belongs to behind the one named next, so that half is written second.

blocks.note: a doe is a female deer, and that sound is spelt the French way here, where eau is said 'oh'
a hamlet is a small village
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver, from the Latin argentum, and it is the pair that goes

annotation.surface: A hamlet with no silver to its name trails a bellowing deer towards the coast of Normandy.
annotation.walkthrough: Hamlet is the settlement, not the prince. Deauville is the smart seaside town on the Normandy coast, known for its racecourse and its film festival.
annotation.definitionFit: Deauville is the fashionable beach town on the Normandy coast, so Normandy resort places it exactly.

entries.clue: Some older van fuel (4)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, and that part is already spelt out there unbroken.

blocks.note: the run crosses the gap between the two words: olDER Van

annotation.surface: The fuel an ageing van runs on.
annotation.walkthrough: DERV is what British pumps call diesel, from Diesel Engined Road Vehicle, and it survives mostly on forecourt signs. Short concealments usually straddle a space, as this one does.
annotation.definitionFit: DERV is the diesel sold for road vehicles, so fuel is the plain category it belongs to.

entries.clue: A place for a tree-lined street (6)

blocks.note: the clue's opening word, taken as the letter it is
the place an event is held is its venue

annotation.surface: Finding somewhere to put a street lined with trees.
annotation.walkthrough: The two indefinite articles do different jobs: the first is a letter of the answer, the second only joins the halves. Avenue came into English as the grand approach to a country house, which is where the trees come from.
annotation.definitionFit: An avenue is a broad road planted with trees along both sides, which is what a tree-lined street describes.

entries.clue: Clean off Roman road around Spanish city (8)

indicatorNotes.off: Milk goes off when it has turned, and letters called off have turned the same way, out of the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.around: Around wraps the piece it follows about the letters just made, so those letters finish in the middle.

blocks.note: via is Latin for road, and the Roman roads carried the word into English
five letters of fodder, which the road then closes around

annotation.surface: Scrubbing down the old Roman road that loops around a city in Spain.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants clean off to mean wipe away; the setter wants off on its own, in the sense that milk goes off. Valencia sits on Spain's Mediterranean coast and gives its name to the orange.
annotation.definitionFit: Valencia is Spain's third city, on the Mediterranean coast, so Spanish city reaches it as one instance of the kind.

entries.clue: Born as required, endlessly (3)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Something endless has no end, so the word in front of it gives up its last letter.

blocks.note: what is required is what somebody must have

annotation.surface: A birth that comes exactly when it is wanted, and goes on for ever.
annotation.walkthrough: Nee is the French for born, the word English keeps for the surname a married woman was born with. The comma is punctuation only, and the instruction reaches back across it.
annotation.definitionFit: Nee is printed before a maiden name to mean born, which is the sense the definition gives.

entries.clue: Former wife’s wrong to gain illegally (6)

blocks.note: ex is what anyone calls a former spouse, and the possessive carries it into the charade
a tort is a civil wrong in law, the kind you are sued over rather than charged with

annotation.surface: Saying the ex-wife is in the wrong for making her money outside the law.
annotation.walkthrough: Wrong is a noun here, not the adjective the surface offers: a tort is negligence or trespass, matter for a claim rather than a prosecution. Ex has meant a former partner far longer than crosswords have used it.
annotation.definitionFit: To extort is to get money out of somebody by threats, which is gaining it illegally.

entries.clue: University composition is read out to the country (inits) (3)

indicatorNotes.read out: Read out means spoken rather than spelt, so the word before it is wanted for the noise it makes.
indicatorNotes.(inits): Inits warns that what goes in the grid is a run of initials rather than a word, which is how three letters can name a whole nation.

blocks.note: U is the standard short form for university on any list of institutions
a composition set at school is an essay, and said aloud that word is the names of two letters

annotation.surface: A college essay being read aloud for the whole nation to hear.
annotation.walkthrough: The trick is that a word's sound can be the names of letters: essay spoken is S then A. Inits is the setter owning up that the entry is a string of initials rather than a word.
annotation.definitionFit: The United States of America is the country meant, and its initials are how the name is ordinarily written.

entries.clue: Drive away fast as it is offensive (9)

blocks.note: to repel an attack is to drive it away
Lent is the forty days of fasting before Easter, the Church's fast

annotation.surface: Clear off quickly, because the thing is objectionable.
annotation.walkthrough: Fast is the noun, not the adverb the surface reads: the Church's fast is Lent. Insect repellent and a repellent remark are one word doing two sorts of work.
annotation.definitionFit: Something repellent drives people off by being distasteful, which is what calling it offensive says.

entries.clue: China clay not completed, rip one apart (9)

indicatorNotes.not completed: Something not completed stops before its end, so the word in front loses its final letter.
indicatorNotes.apart: Things taken apart come to pieces, and letters in pieces are put back in an order of the setter's choosing.

blocks.note: clay with its last letter cut off, three letters of fodder
three more letters of fodder, taken as written
the word itself, filling out the nine

annotation.surface: A half-finished piece of pottery clay, and an order to tear one of them up.
annotation.walkthrough: China clay is a real material, the white kaolin the Potteries are built on, and the surface leans on that to hide the fact that only the first word defines. The comma is punctuation, nothing more.
annotation.definitionFit: Porcelain is the fine white ceramic England named china after the country it was shipped from, so china is the everyday word for the same stuff.

entries.clue: Preserve half the sausages? (4)

indicatorNotes.half: Half asks for one of the word's two halves, and with nothing said about which, it is the front one.

blocks.note: saveloys are the bright red, ready-cooked pork sausages sold in British chip shops

annotation.surface: Keeping half the sausages back for later.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the sausage as a for-instance, one kind among many, rather than a definition of anything. An eight-letter word split down the middle is the tidiest halving a setter gets.
annotation.definitionFit: To save something is to keep it from being used up or lost, which is preserve in its everyday sense.

entries.clue: Exchange coaches without one official returning (8)

indicatorNotes.without: Without means going short of, so the letter named next is taken out of the word before it.
indicatorNotes.returning: Something returning comes back the way it went, so the letters just found are written in reverse.

blocks.note: to coach a team is to train it
I is the Roman numeral for one, and it is the letter that goes
the ref is the official who runs a football or rugby match

annotation.surface: Swapping the coaching staff about while one of the officials heads back.
annotation.walkthrough: Coaches is the verb rather than the buses or the railway carriages the surface offers. A club transfers a player between sides, which is what keeps the sporting surface upright.
annotation.definitionFit: To transfer something is to hand it over to another place or owner, which is the move exchange names.

entries.clue: Come to understand there's a number not at home (6,3)

blocks.note: a figure is a numeral, as in the figure written on a cheque
someone out is not at home, the answer given at the door

annotation.surface: Realising that one of the house numbers has nobody in.
annotation.walkthrough: Out for away from home is the oldest sense of the word, the one a neighbour uses on the doorstep. The enumeration splitting six and three is the only sign that two words are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: To figure something out is to work at it until you grasp it, which is coming to understand it.

entries.clue: Mischievous child with cord, right and wrong (8)

blocks.note: an imp is a small mischievous sprite, and the word is used of any naughty child
a cord is a length of rope
R is the standard short form for right, as in a stage direction

annotation.surface: A naughty child with a piece of rope, and an argument about right and wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: Right earns a letter and wrong is the definition, so the two halves of one stock phrase are doing opposite jobs. Imp was a small demon in folklore long before it softened into a word for a child.
annotation.definitionFit: Improper behaviour breaks the rules of decency, so wrong names it in the moral sense rather than the mistaken one.

entries.clue: Plodding to wood circle, not right (9)

indicatorNotes.not: Not takes away what it names, so the letter that follows is missing from the piece just found.

blocks.note: lumber is sawn timber, the American word for wood
a ring is a circle drawn or worn
R is the standard short form for right, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: Trudging towards a ring of trees that is not quite right.
annotation.walkthrough: Lumbering for moving heavily and slowly has nothing to do with the timber the word is built from here; the two senses reached English by separate routes. Right is R, one of the busiest single letters in the box.
annotation.definitionFit: A lumbering walk is slow and heavy-footed, which is the gait plodding describes.

entries.clue: Composes legal actions in English? On the contrary (6)

indicatorNotes.in: In would put the piece before it inside the piece after it, which is the instruction the next three words turn round.
indicatorNotes.On the contrary: On the contrary denies the arrangement just described, so the piece that was to go inside is the one that opens up instead.

blocks.note: a writ is the document that starts a legal action, and several of them are writs
E is the standard short form for English on a list of languages

annotation.surface: The suggestion that the lawsuits are being brought in English, promptly contradicted.
annotation.walkthrough: On the contrary is an instruction, not a comment: it swaps the two halves of the containment the clue has just set up. Writs are the papers that open a case in court.
annotation.definitionFit: To write a letter or a song is to compose it, so composes is the same act in the same tense.

entries.clue: Animal's lair is in decay (6)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the piece before it inside the word that follows, which splits open to take it.

blocks.note: to rot is to decay
a den is the lair a fox or a badger lives in

annotation.surface: A creature's den slowly falling to pieces.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is standing in for is, which is what lets the clue read as a sentence rather than a list. Rodent covers the gnawing mammals, so the definition is the family and not any one of its members.
annotation.definitionFit: A rodent is any of the gnawing mammals, rats and mice among them, so animal is the broad class it sits in.

entries.clue: Be dreary? No use your loaf! (3,5)

annotation.definitionNote: Use your loaf is an order to think rather than a noun; the setter is allowed it because the phrase turns on the literal loaf, which is what the answer is.

indicatorNotes.No: No refuses the letters in the order they have just been given, which is the setter's way of asking for them in another.

blocks.note: two letters of fodder
six more, filling out the eight

annotation.surface: Told sharply that being dull is no substitute for thinking.
annotation.walkthrough: Use your loaf is Cockney rhyming slang, loaf of bread for head, so the phrase means think. The setter takes the loaf at face value and asks for the bread instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Rye bread is sold as a loaf, and the definition reaches it by reading the slang literally rather than as the head it stands for.

entries.clue: Roger endlessly troubled so (4)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Endlessly means without its end, so the name drops its last letter before anything else is done to it.
indicatorNotes.troubled: Something troubled is unsettled, and unsettled letters will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: Roger with its final letter gone, the four that are left

annotation.surface: A man called Roger, forever bothered by something.
annotation.walkthrough: Ergo is Latin for therefore, kept in English for the mock-formal flourish at the end of an argument. Roger is the name here, not the radio operator's yes.
annotation.definitionFit: Ergo introduces a conclusion, therefore or and so, which is the sense of so that ties one statement to the next.

entries.clue: British city with verve (4)

blocks.note: B is the standard short form for British
Rio de Janeiro, shortened to its first word as everybody shortens it

annotation.surface: A city in Britain with plenty of spirit about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The city is Brazilian, not British: only the first word gives a letter and the wordplay then goes abroad. Brio is the musical direction con brio, played with spirit.
annotation.definitionFit: Brio is dash and energy in performance, as in a pianist playing with brio, which is what verve names.

entries.clue: Can one batting first find kitchen gadget? (3-6)

blocks.note: a tin of beans is a can
in cricket the openers are the two batsmen who go in at the start of an innings

annotation.surface: Asking whether the batsman who goes in first can lay hands on a kitchen gadget.
annotation.walkthrough: Can is the tin rather than the question the sentence seems to be putting, which is why the clue can end in a question mark at all. Opener is doing the same trick from the other side.
annotation.definitionFit: A tin-opener is the handheld tool for cutting the lid off a can, kept in every kitchen drawer.

entries.clue: Denial from leading actress in New York (3)

indicatorNotes.leading: The leading letter of a word is the one at its front, and that one letter is all that is wanted.
indicatorNotes.in: In drops the letter just found inside the pair that follows, which parts to take it.

blocks.note: NY is the postal short form for New York
the front letter of actress

annotation.surface: A refusal from the star of a New York show.
annotation.walkthrough: Leading is the trap: it reads as top billing and asks for a single letter. Nay is the old word for no, kept alive by the ayes and the noes of a parliamentary vote.
annotation.definitionFit: To say nay is to refuse or deny something, which is the denial the definition means.

entries.clue: Love the French matador's cry (3)

blocks.note: love is a score of nothing in tennis, written as the round O
le is one of the French words for the

annotation.surface: Declaring a fondness for the shout a French bullfighter gives.
annotation.walkthrough: The French words for the are among the commonest imports in a grid, and only the crossing letters say which of them is wanted. Ole is called out at every pass of the cape, by the crowd as much as the man.
annotation.definitionFit: Ole is the shout that greets a good pass in the bullring, so a matador's cry names it by the occasion it belongs to.

entries.clue: Those who speak of a crime novelist? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: Those who speak is plural and a crime novelist is one person; the setter is allowed both because the novelist's surname is spelt exactly like the plural noun.

blocks.note: a sayer is one who says something, the word that survives inside naysayer and soothsayer
the between-the-wars writer of the Lord Peter Wimsey mysteries, her given names Dorothy L

annotation.surface: People gossiping about a writer of murder mysteries.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the novelist as a for-instance, one crime writer among many, picked because her name is also an ordinary word. Of is the join and does nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: Sayers are people who say things, the plural of sayer; Dorothy L Sayers wrote the Wimsey mysteries, so a crime novelist reaches the same spelling by example.

entries.clue: Stationery found in cheapo stitchwork (4-2)

indicatorNotes.found in: Found in says the letters are already sitting in the words that follow, written out in order with nothing changed.

blocks.note: the run straddles the gap between the two words: cheaPO STITchwork

annotation.surface: Office supplies turning up inside a piece of cheap needlework.
annotation.walkthrough: A concealment needs an unlikely phrase to hide in, and cheapo stitchwork is built for the job rather than said by anybody. The hyphen in the enumeration belongs to the trade name.
annotation.definitionFit: A Post-it is the small sticky note sold in pads, stationery of the everyday desk-drawer sort.
